title: The Adi Granth installed, 1604
hookLine: the book is placed in the Harmandir and Baba Buddha reads the first hukam

cards: The book is finished. Page after page, written by hand, every hymn set under its raga. Now what?

You could put it on a shelf, or keep it in the Guru's own room. Guru Arjan did neither. In 1604 the book was carried in procession to the Harmandir Sahib, the house with four doors in the middle of the pool.
Tradition says the old man Baba Buddha, who had known Guru Nanak as a boy, carried it on his head, and the Guru walked behind with a whisk, waving it over the book the way you'd honor a king.

teach.b: Adi means first, or original. Granth means book. The first book: that's what Sikhs call the volume Guru Arjan compiled.
Much later it would become the Guru Granth Sahib, a story for another day. Now watch what happens in the Harmandir.

teach.h: THE GURU SITS LOWER THAN THE BOOK.
teach.b: The book is placed on a raised seat in the center, under a canopy, and the Guru sits below it. The man who made it takes a humbler place than the words.
Baba Buddha is named the first granthi, the keeper and reader of the book. Then comes a moment Sikhs still repeat each day. He opens the book at random and reads the hymn at the top of the left page.

teach.h: A HUKAM, A WORD FOR THE DAY.
teach.b: That reading is called a hukam, an order, or a word for the day. Tradition says the very first hukam was a line of Guru Arjan's own, saying in plain words that God himself stands up to carry out the work of the saints.
A fitting word for a new house. The practice goes on in gurdwaras all over the world: every morning the book is opened, and a random hymn is read as the word for the day.
Some Sikhs look up the Harmandir Sahib's hukam on their phones before breakfast. A practice from 1604, in your pocket. The words were gathered, sorted and guarded.
Now they have a home, a keeper, and a voice.

how: Every day in gurdwaras, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened and a hymn read at random as the hukam, the day's word; the hukam from the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is shared widely each morning.

games.why: tradition says the Guru sat below the book: the words took the higher place, and the man who gathered them sat beneath.

practice: Let any book near you fall open, a novel, a cookbook, a book of poems, a holy book if you have one, and read the first line your eye lands on, slowly, twice.
Then close it and sit with the line, the way a room full of people sits with the day's hukam. It may mean nothing, or it may land exactly; let it be the word you were handed.
